title: Biological Physics
text:
FYS3715 · Spring 2027 · University of Oslo
    How does a bacterium find food in a world without inertia? Why does a cell burst in pure water?
       How can entropy create order? And how do identical cells organise themselves into a tissue with a shape?
In this course you use statistical physics, soft matter and mechanics to build quantitative models of living systems on scales from 1 nm to a few hundred micrometres. You test the models against your own measurements and simulations.

title: Biological Physics
text:
How the course works

Lectures on Tuesdays and Thursdays 10–12 follow the three blocks above.
A weekly exercise (about 2 h) is due on Wednesday and reviewed on Thursday. Ten of thirteen must be passed.
Three projects on current research problems using real research tools. P1 is the same for everyone. P2 and P3 are chosen from the electives. Each project ends with a report and an oral defense, where you present your result and are questioned on your understanding of it.
LLMs are expected tools in this course, for analysis and for writing. See Working with LLMs. What is assessed is what you understand, and that is checked orally.
Final oral exam in June sets the grade.

The textbook is Philip Nelson, Biological Physics: Energy, Information, Life, chapters 1–7 and 11.1–11.2. The week-by-week plan is in the schedule.

title: C: Morphogenesis, mechanobiology and imaging
text:
How do identical cells organise themselves into a tissue with a shape? How do cells feel and respond to forces? We look at active materials that shape themselves, the cytoskeleton and adhesion, the physics of adherent cells, differential adhesion and the Cellular Potts model, Turing patterns versus positional information, and the new microscopy that lets us see living tissue without labels.
This block is being moved to the new format.

title: Lab: Brownian motion
text: The purpose of this lab is to learn some basic statistical physics, microscopy, imaging and image analysis. The data you take here are the data for Project 1. The theory is in the notes on active and passive motion, sections on random walks, diffusion, viscous drag and the Langevin equation.

title: Lab: Brownian motion
text:
Background

Nobel Prize in 2009
Electronic cameras surround us everywhere and have been used scientifically since they were invented. In 2009, Willard S. Boyle and George E. Smith at Bell Laboratories were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics “for the invention of an imaging semiconductor circuit, the CCD sensor”.


The optical microscope
The microscope is a stable stand that allows small, controlled movements of what you are looking at relative to the light source and the objective. The illumination is at least as important for what you see as the type of objective you use. If the illumination is correct, the resolution of the microscope is set by the numerical aperture (NA) of the objective. The resolution is the radius of the diffraction pattern from point sources, and is at best \(r=\lambda/(2\,\mathrm{NA})\), where \(\lambda\) is the wavelength of the light. We have two objectives with NA = 0.4 and NA = 0.65, so the resolutions for green light are \(D_{20X}=0.7\) µm and \(D_{40X}=0.4\) µm.


Imaging with electronic cameras
The objective sends out an almost parallel beam of rays. This beam must pass through an eyepiece to form an image on the retina, or through an imaging lens to form an image on the sensor of a camera. In an electronic camera, electrons are released where light falls on a semiconductor chip. The chip is divided into many pixels, each of which works as a light sensor.

The spatial resolution of a camera is set by how many pixels the chip is divided into.
Just as important is the intensity resolution: how many intensity levels each pixel can distinguish. It depends on the pixel size (larger pixels collect more electrons), the sensor temperature (fewer thermal noise electrons when cold) and the readout noise (usually larger for faster readout). Most simple cameras and image formats use \(2^8=256\) levels (8 bit). Good SLR cameras have a raw format with 12 bit (\(2^{12}=4096\) levels). Good scientific cameras are cooled to between −80 and −180 °C and have expensive readout electronics giving \(2^{16}=65536\) levels. Then each pixel is an accurate, sensitive light meter.
Square pixels are an advantage: the conversion from pixels to object size is then the same horizontally and vertically.
If you do not need colour information, a greyscale camera is better, because colour filtering costs both spatial and intensity resolution.
The last choice is the chip technology, CCD or CMOS.



Image analysis






Figure 1: Analysis of an imaged square grid. Top left: monochrome image of a square grid with 50 µm between the lines and 5 µm wide lines. Top right: the same image as a matrix \(I\), shown as a colour map. Note that the element \(I[0,0]\) is in the upper left corner. Bottom: vertical cross-section I[:, 500] on the left and horizontal cross-section I[500, :] on the right.



We only use monochrome cameras here. A monochrome image is a 2D matrix with elements \(I_{ij}\), \(i=1\ldots N_y\), \(j=1\ldots N_x\). For an 8-bit image, \(I_{ij}\) is between 0 (black) and 255 (white). The pixel coordinates correspond to object coordinates \(x_j=j s_x\) and \(y_i=i s_y\), where \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) are the pixel sizes in the object (µm per pixel). One of the first things to do with a new imaging system is to find \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) by imaging an object of known size and counting how many pixels it covers.
Figure 1 shows a greyscale image with 1024 × 1280 pixels and intensities between 50 and 240. The positions of the horizontal lines are the 4 minima in the lower left plot, and the positions of the vertical lines are the 5 minima in the lower right plot. Since the lines are 50 µm apart, these minima give \(s_x\) and \(s_y\).
In Python:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image

I = np.array(Image.open('grid20x.png').convert('L'))  # greyscale matrix
plt.imshow(I, cmap='gray'); plt.colorbar()
plt.figure(); plt.plot(I[:, 500]); plt.plot(I[500, :])

title: Lab: Brownian motion
text:
Before the lab

Install Python with numpy, scipy, matplotlib, pandas, trackpy and pims (see Working with LLMs for how to get help with this).
Run randomwalk_exercise.py a few times. Change timesteps, numpart and stepsize and see how the result changes.
Run synthetic_brownian.py. It makes a movie of simulated beads with a known \(D\), tracks it with trackpy, and prints the true and the fitted \(D\). This is the reference you will test your own pipeline against.

title: Lab: Brownian motion
text:
In the lab

Imaging quality and calibration
Get help to place the test slide in the microscope, turn on the light, open the camera program, and set the camera to take pictures continuously and show them on the screen. Never touch the surface of the test slide!

Use the 20X objective, find a field with a square grid, and focus while looking in the eyepiece.
Open a window that shows the histogram and a window where you can set the exposure time. The histogram shows how many pixels have each intensity. You should see two peaks, one for the white stripes and one for the black stripes.
Set a light intensity that is comfortable for the eyes. Then adjust the focus and the exposure time to get the largest possible distance between the two peaks in the histogram. You now have maximum contrast.
Save a still image of the grid and determine \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) as in Figure 1.
Repeat for the 40X objective.
Is the resolution limited by diffraction or by the camera pixels? Calculate \(D_{20X}/s_x\) and \(D_{40X}/s_x\) and explain what these ratios tell you.
Optional: Modulation transfer function (MTF). With the 20X objective, focus on the field with 60 LP/mm (line pairs per millimetre) and optimise contrast. Save an image, plot an intensity profile normal to the stripes, and note \(I_{\min}\) and \(I_{\max}\). Repeat with 380, 500 and 600 LP/mm, and then with the 40X objective. Plot \(\mathrm{MTF}(f)=(I_{\max}(f)-I_{\min}(f))/(I_{\max}(60)-I_{\min}(60))\) for both objectives.



Brownian motion
Get help from a supervisor to prepare a microscope slide with a small volume of liquid containing small particles. Use the 20X objective and normal illumination to find an area with particles. Switch to dark-field illumination if it is difficult to find the particles.

Take one picture of the particles with normal illumination and one with dark-field illumination, with the best contrast you can get. Describe the difference between the two images and how each is produced.
Determine the mean particle size in pixels and in micrometres. Compare with the nominal bead size and with the resolution of the objective.
Record a 30 s movie at 15 frames per second with the best contrast and focus. Play it a few times (e.g. in ImageJ/Fiji) to see roughly how far the most mobile particles move during the movie.
Before you leave: run trackpy.locate on one frame and trackpy.annotate to check that the particles are found (see trackpy_anal.ipynb). It is much easier to fix exposure and focus now than to rescue bad data later.
Record a 5 min movie at 15 frames per second with the best possible contrast and focus.
Write down: objective, pixel size, frame rate, exposure time, bead size (nominal), temperature in the room, and anything that may cause drift (evaporation, a tilted stage, a warm lamp).



After the lab
The analysis is Project 1. A short image sequence from an earlier lab, cropped to 1024 × 1024 pixels, is in src/stack2_crop/ if you want to start testing before you have your own data.

title: E5: Active Brownian particles and the Vicsek model
text:
1. One active Brownian particle
Simulate 400 independent active Brownian particles with the finite-difference equations in the notes, using \(v = 1\), \(D_T = 0.1\), \(D_R = 0.5\), \(\Delta t = 0.01\) (arbitrary units) and \(2\times10^4\) time steps. Plot the MSD against time on log–log axes.

Identify the diffusive, ballistic and enhanced-diffusive regimes. At what times do the crossovers happen? Compare with \(D_T/v^2\) and \(\tau_R = 1/D_R\).
Compare the long-time slope with \(D_{\rm eff} = D_T + v^2\tau_R/2\).
crumbs: E5: Active Brownian particles and the Vicsek model

title: E5: Active Brownian particles and the Vicsek model
text:
2. The flocking transition
Use vicsek_model.generate_vicsek_data (see vicsek_model_exercise.py) with \(N = 400\), \(L = 14\) (density \(\approx 2\)), \(r = 1\), \(v = 0.1\) and 500 iterations.

For noise amplitudes \(\eta = 0.1, 0.2, \ldots, 1.0\), compute the order parameter \(\psi = \frac{1}{N}\left|\sum_i \mathbf v_i / v\right|\), averaged over the last 200 iterations. Plot \(\psi\) against \(\eta\).
Where is the transition? Run once more at the \(\eta\) closest to the transition. How much does \(\psi\) fluctuate in time there, compared with far from it?
Why is \(\psi \approx 1/\sqrt{N}\), not 0, in the disordered phase?

Generate synthetic data \(y = a t + b + \text{noise}\) with \(a = 2\), \(b = 0.5\), 30 points for \(t\in[0,10]\) and Gaussian noise with standard deviation 1. title: Active matter: lecture notes
text:
Active matter systems consume energy from their environment and use it as fuel to propel themselves and drive themselves far from equilibrium. Examples: living organisms and artificial machines (micro-robots, artificial molecular machines, etc.).
Because of their intrinsic activity, these systems can spontaneously show complex patterns of motion, such as swarming or flocking. This is associated with an emergent global order from the self-organization of the constituents of active matter.
Emergent (self-organized) behaviour occurs at many different scales. Some of these patterns turn out to be robust and universal: they are independent of the type of animal that makes up the swarm.



School of fish

E. coli swarming

Cell migration

We can model the universal swarming behaviour of self-propelled (active) particles with several minimal statistical models.
In this lecture we introduce a few minimal models of active particles. If we get to it, we will also discuss different kinds of order (polar versus nematic) that emerge from collective interactions of active particles.

title: Active matter: lecture notes
text:
Single active particles: self-propelled Brownians

Self-propulsion is common in living organisms. It allows a more efficient exploration of the environment when looking for nutrients or running away from toxic substances.
A paradigmatic example is the swimming of bacteria such as E. coli. It resembles the motion of a passive Brownian particle, but it also has an active component due to self-propulsion.
We call them self-propelled Brownians, because they meander but also propel themselves by taking up energy from their environment and converting it into directed motion.
Self-propelled Brownians = random meandering + active swimming




Self-propulsion speed as a function of the size of a microswimmer.





Random trajectory of a run-and-tumble particle (RTP) versus an active Brownian particle (ABP).



Active Brownian particles
This is like an overdamped (no inertia) Brownian particle with two kinds of motion:

random meandering like a passive Brownian particle, with a noise amplitude set by the translational diffusivity \(D_T\);
self-propulsion with a constant speed \(v\), but in a random direction \(\theta\). The randomness in the orientation of the self-propulsion has a noise amplitude set by the rotational diffusivity \(D_R\).

For motion confined to the \(xy\)-plane, the active Brownian particle is modelled by 3 dynamical variables \((x(t),y(t),\theta(t))\): its position and the angle of the self-propulsion velocity. The dynamical equations for these variables are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot x &= v\cos\theta +\sqrt{2D_T}\,\xi_x, \quad \langle\xi_x\rangle = 0,\quad \langle\xi_x(t)\xi_x(t')\rangle =\delta(t-t')\\
\dot y &= v\sin\theta +\sqrt{2D_T}\,\xi_y, \quad \langle\xi_y\rangle = 0,\quad \langle\xi_y(t)\xi_y(t')\rangle =\delta(t-t')\\
\dot \theta &= \sqrt{2D_R}\,\xi_\theta, \quad \langle\xi_\theta\rangle = 0,\quad \langle\xi_\theta(t)\xi_\theta(t')\rangle =\delta(t-t')
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]

Overdamped motion
We can rewrite the equations of motion in vector form. Then it becomes clearer that this is overdamped motion, with drag coefficient \(\gamma\):
\[
\gamma\dot{\mathbf r} = F\hat{\mathbf e} +\boldsymbol{\xi}
\]


Finite-difference equations
These equations are usually solved numerically in discrete time, with \(\Delta t\) the time increment between successive times, \(t_{n+1} = t_n+\Delta t\). The corresponding finite-difference equations are
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{n+1} &= x_n+v\cos\theta_n\Delta t+\sqrt{2D_T \Delta t}\,W_{x,n}\\
y_{n+1} &= y_n+v\sin\theta_n\Delta t+\sqrt{2D_T \Delta t}\,W_{y,n}\\
\theta_{n+1} &= \theta_n+\sqrt{2D_R \Delta t}\,W_{\theta,n}
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]
where \(W_{x}, W_{y}, W_\theta\) are Gaussian random numbers with zero mean and unit standard deviation, drawn independently at each time step.



Run-and-tumble
The run-and-tumble model was inspired by chemotaxis of bacteria, that is, how bacteria move towards or away from a food source.



Run and tumble modes.


The particle alternates between an active state, where it moves with constant speed \(v\) in a given direction (“run”), and a passive state, where its position stays the same but its orientation keeps changing (“tumble”). The change in direction is taken as instantaneous and occurs with a given rate \(\lambda/\Delta t\), so that the particle moves along a straight line between successive tumbles. The “run” state is punctuated at random times by an instantaneous “tumble” (reorientation). This is modelled as a Poisson point process, characterised by the Poisson distribution
\[
P_\lambda(n) = \frac{\lambda^n}{n!}e^{-\lambda},
\]
where \(n= 0,1,2,\ldots\) is the number of tumbling events observed in a time interval \(\Delta t\), and \(\lambda\) is the average number of tumbling events expected in \(\Delta t\).
Notice that \(P(n=0) = e^{-\lambda}\) is the probability of no tumbling in a time interval \(\Delta t\). We therefore introduce the probability of tumbling in a time interval \(\Delta t\) as \(P_{\rm tumble} = 1-e^{-\lambda}\), and the probability of running as \(P_{\rm run} = P(n=0) = e^{-\lambda}\).
Now we can model the motion of a single bacterium in the plane with 4 dynamical variables \((x,y,\theta,\rho)\). The additional variable \(\rho\) keeps track of the state of the bacterium (1: run, 0: tumble).
The finite-difference evolution equations for these variables are
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{n+1}&= x_n+\rho_n v\cos\theta_n \Delta t+\sqrt{2D_T \Delta t}\,W_{x,n}\\
y_{n+1}&= y_n+\rho_n v\sin\theta_n \Delta t+\sqrt{2D_T \Delta t}\,W_{y,n}\\
\theta_{n+1}&= \theta_n+(1-\rho_n)\Delta \theta_n\\
\rho_{n+1} &= \begin{cases} 0 & \text{with probability } 1-e^{-\lambda} \\
1 & \text{with probability } e^{-\lambda}
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]
where \(W_{x}, W_{y}\) are Gaussian random numbers with zero mean and unit standard deviation, drawn independently at each time step, and \(\Delta\theta_n\) is the random reorientation during a tumble.


Diffusive behaviour of self-propelled Brownians
Let us introduce the characteristic time scale of rotational diffusion (meandering), \(\tau_R = 1/D_R\). On time scales much longer than \(\tau_R\), the self-propelled Brownian particle diffuses with an effective diffusivity that is larger than the thermal diffusivity:
\[
D_{\rm eff} = D_T+ \frac{v^2\tau_R}{2}
\tag{4}\]



The mean square displacement as a function of time has three characteristic regimes: (i) passive diffusion on very short time scales, (ii) an intermediate ballistic regime, and (iii) diffusion with enhanced diffusivity on long time scales.


\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle(\Delta r)^2\rangle (t)&= \langle(\Delta x)^2\rangle(t)+\langle(\Delta y)^2\rangle(t)\\
\langle(\Delta r)^2\rangle (t)&= \begin{cases}
4D_T t+v^2t^2, & t\ll \tau_R\\
(4D_T +2v^2\tau_R)\,t, & t\gg \tau_R
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]
The effective diffusion coefficient is
\[
D_{\rm eff}= \lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\langle|\Delta r|^2\rangle}{4t} = D_T+\frac{v^2 \tau_R}{2}
\]

title: Active matter: lecture notes
section: Interacting self-propelled Brownians: the Vicsek model for swarming
text:
Interacting self-propelled Brownians: the Vicsek model for swarming
Vicsek et al. (1995) published a minimal model for flocking due to alignment interactions between neighbouring particles.
For simplicity, consider active particles moving in the plane. Each of them is described by its coordinates \((x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})\) and its orientation of motion \(\theta^{(i)}\), where \(i\) is the particle label.



Reorientation in the Vicsek model.



Finite-difference equations
The finite-difference evolution equations for particle \(i\) are
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{n+1}^{(i)} &= x_n^{(i)}+v\cos\theta^{(i)}_n\Delta t\\
y_{n+1}^{(i)} &= y_n^{(i)}+v\sin\theta^{(i)}_n\Delta t\\
\theta_{n+1}^{(i)} &= \langle\theta_n^{(j)}\rangle_{S_i}+\sqrt{2D_R\Delta t}\, W_{\theta^{(i)},n}
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\]
where \(\langle\theta_n^{(j)}\rangle_{S_i}\) is the average orientation of all the active particles in the neighbourhood \(S_i\) of the \(i\)-th particle (see the illustration above). In the original paper the noise is uniform, \(\eta\,U(-\pi,\pi)\); the code we use in the lab follows the paper.


Numerical examples showing the emergence of polar order (flocking)

Vicsek model with interaction radius \(R_1 = 0.1 L\) and higher noise.

Vicsek model with a larger interaction radius \(R_2 = 0.2 L\) and higher noise.

Vicsek model with \(R_1\) and lower noise.

title: Active matter: lecture notes
section: Emergent nematic order in bacterial colonies
text:
Emergent nematic order in bacterial colonies
Bacteria are elongated particles with rod-like shapes. When they are closely packed, they tend to align their principal axes along a preferred orientation. In doing so, they break rotational symmetry (all directions equally accessible) and form an ordered state with a preferred orientation. This is called nematic order.



Snapshots of a growing bacterial colony in which bacteria self-organise and align their orientation in a preferred direction.


Nematic order is commonly found in passive systems known as liquid crystals. By analogy, active matter with nematic order is often called an active liquid crystal.
Polar versus nematic order:



Polar versus nematic order.

title: Active matter: lecture notes
section: Polar ordering of epithelial cell layers
text:
Polar ordering of epithelial cell layers

Epithelial cells
From Wikipedia: a thin, continuous, protective layer of compactly packed cells with little intercellular matrix. Epithelial tissues line the outer surfaces of organs and blood vessels throughout the body, as well as the inner surfaces of cavities in many internal organs.



Types of epithelium (Wikimedia Commons).





Topological defects



Typical topological defects observed in a liquid crystal sample. Each defect has a topological charge \(s\), defined as the number of times the vector field winds around a loop encircling the defect once in the anticlockwise sense. Hence (a) and (b) have \(s = +1\), (c) \(s = -1\), (d) \(s = +1/2\), (e) \(s=-1/2\).




Flow and polar ordering
Integer topological defect annihilations drive polar ordering of epithelial monolayers, Emma Lång, Anna Lång, Pernille Blicher, Torbjørn Rognes, Paul Dommersnes, Stig Ove Bøe.



From Lång et al.



a: Time evolution of polar ordering. The colour map represents the angle of the local velocity field relative to the \(x\)-axis. The surface of a whole circular monolayer is shown. Scale bar, 1 mm.
b: Detection and mapping of ±1 topological defects.
h: Time series showing annihilation of a ±1 topological defect pair. Scale bar, 100 µm.



Active elastic solid model
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot{\mathbf R}_i&=V_c\mathbf P_i+\frac{1}{\xi}\mathbf F_i\\
\dot{\mathbf P}_i&=\gamma(\mathbf P_i\times\dot{\mathbf R}_i)\times\mathbf P_i
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\]
Here \(\mathbf R_i\) is the position of cell \(i\) and \(\mathbf P_i\) the polarity of cell propulsion (the direction of propulsion). \(V_c\) is the cell propulsion speed in the absence of elastic forces, \(\mathbf F_i\) the elastic force on the cell, and \(\xi\) the substrate friction. The first equation expresses the balance of forces. The second gives the polar ordering effect: the direction of propulsion turns towards the direction of motion with rate constant \(\gamma\).

title: P1: Measuring Boltzmann’s constant with a microscope
text:
In 1908 Jean Perrin used Brownian motion to measure Avogadro’s number, and with it Boltzmann’s constant. You will do the same with beads in water, a microscope and a camera. Your question is:

How well can you determine \(k_B\) from the Brownian motion of beads, and what limits the accuracy?

The physics is in the notes on active and passive motion: random walks, the diffusion equation, Stokes drag, the Langevin equation and the Einstein relation \(\xi D = k_BT\). The data come from the Brownian motion lab.

title: P1: Measuring Boltzmann’s constant with a microscope
text:
What the project should contain

1. Measurement

Track the beads in your 5 min movie: locate, link, filter out short tracks and stuck particles, and subtract drift.
Plot the ensemble MSD \(\langle \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2\rangle\) against lag time on linear axes and fit a straight line. Explain what the slope and the intercept mean.
From the slope get \(D\). Then use the Einstein relation with Stokes drag, \(D = k_BT/(6\pi\eta r)\), to get \(k_B\), with an uncertainty.



2. Three checks that the result is right
Getting trackpy to give a number is easy, with or without an LLM. Showing that the number is right is the project. Include all three checks:

Synthetic ground truth. Make a synthetic movie with known \(D\) and the same pixel size, frame rate, particle size and contrast as your data (use synthetic_brownian.py, or write your own and explain it). Run exactly your pipeline on it. Do you get back the \(D\) you put in? If not, your pipeline is wrong on the real data too.
Physical expectation. Before you trust a fit, calculate the \(D\) you expect from the nominal bead size, the viscosity of water at the lab temperature and the known \(k_B\). Is your measured value close? If not, why?
Sensitivity. Show how \(D\) changes when you vary the key parameters: minmass, search_range, the minimum track length and the range of lag times in the fit. Argue why your chosen values are defensible.



3. Model comparison
Compare with a random-walk simulation (for example randomwalk_exercise.py). What step length and time step must the random walk have to match your experiment? Why does the mass of the bead not appear in the result?


4. Physics and biology

Show that the beads are at low Reynolds number and that inertia is irrelevant on the time scale of your frames.
Discuss one biological consequence of diffusion, for example how long it takes a protein to cross a cell, or the oxygen supply limit for a bacterium.

title: Physics of active and passive motion in biology
text:
Random walks
A random walk is a model of a fundamental physical process in which a random walker (a particle, an atom, a measurement, an individual) moves in random steps. A typical example is the Brownian motion of small particles due to the thermal motion of atoms. Another example is the spreading of an atom throughout a fluid.
A random walker in 1D moves \(N\) steps back and forth and has random probability of moving left or right. None of the steps are correlated, the step length is \(d\) and the \(i\)-th step is thus \(u_i=\pm d\). The position after \(n\) steps is thus
\[
x_n=x_0+\sum_{i=1}^n u_i
\tag{1}\]
The ensemble average of the displacement over a large number of walkers is
\[
\langle x_n-x_0\rangle=\Big\langle \sum_{i=1}^n u_i\Big\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^n\langle u_i\rangle=0.
\tag{2}\]
The mean square displacement (MSD) is
\[
\langle (x_n-x_0)^2\rangle=\Big\langle \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n u_i\Big)^2\Big\rangle
=\Big\langle \sum_{i=1}^n u_i\sum_{j=1}^n u_j\Big\rangle
= \sum_{i=1}^n\langle u_i^2 \rangle+ \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j\neq i}\langle u_iu_j\rangle=nd^2.
\tag{3}\]
The last sum equals zero because the steps are uncorrelated. This equation says that the mean square displacement increases linearly with the number of steps \(n\) and that the slope of this linear relation is \(d^2\).
Two Python scripts go with this section:

randomwalk_1d.py is a 1D random walk simulation. It shows the position distribution and the cumulative position distribution at the final time step, and the mean square displacement of the walkers.
randomwalk_exercise.py is a very simple random walk in the \(xy\)-plane. Walkers are placed randomly in part of the plane and then moved in a random direction, with a normally distributed step length, over a given number of time steps. The step length is chosen so that the simulation resembles what you see in the microscope in the lab. The MSD shown at the end is calculated from about 4 times as many particles as those shown in the box. The positions of the particles in the box are also stored, and this list has the same structure as the list of particle positions you will get from the lab experiment.
crumbs: Physics of active and passive motion in biology

title: Physics of active and passive motion in biology
text:
Diffusion
Diffusion is the mixing of a substance that is unevenly distributed in a medium (gas, liquid or solid). The diffusion equation (here in one dimension) states that the flux \(J\) of the substance is proportional to the gradient of the local density, or concentration \(\rho=n/V\), of the substance:
\[
J=-D\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x},
\tag{4}\]
where the diffusion coefficient \(D\) is the proportionality constant. The conservation of matter (matter cannot appear or disappear) is expressed by the continuity equation:
\[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial J}{\partial x}=0
\tag{5}\]
Combine the two to get the partial differential equation for diffusion:
\[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}=D\frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial x^2}
\tag{6}\]
Start with all particles at \(x=0\) at time \(t=0\): \(\rho(t=0,x)=\delta(x)\), where \(\delta\) is the Dirac delta function. Then the diffusion equation has the solution (you may easily verify this)
\[
\rho(t,x)= \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}}\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{4Dt}\right)
\tag{7}\]
This is a Gaussian distribution with mean \(x=0\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{2Dt}\). Thus the width of the distribution is proportional to the square root of the diffusion coefficient. When data are sparse and noisy, one always gets a more precise estimate of the width by integrating over all the data. The second moment of the distribution is
\[
\langle x^2\rangle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^2\rho(t,x)\,dx= 2Dt,
\tag{8}\]
where I have used that
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^2e^{-x^2/a}\,dx= \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}a^{3/2}.
\]






Important



This result, that the mean square displacement \(\langle x^2\rangle=2Dt\), shows how the random walk and Brownian motion are linked to diffusion. In \(d\) dimensions, \(\langle r^2\rangle=2dDt\); in the microscope we measure in 2D, so \(\langle x^2+y^2\rangle=4Dt\).

title: Physics of active and passive motion in biology
text:
Viscous drag

Viscosity
What is viscosity?






Figure 2: Viscosity.





Viscous drag on a particle
Drag is the force \(F_d\) from the fluid on a body moving with velocity \(v\). You can also think of \(F_d\) as the force you need to pull on the particle to keep it at a constant velocity \(v\). When biking on a flat road, the force you put into your pedals to keep a constant speed is almost equal to the drag force of the air on your body.






Figure 3: Drag.



What physical quantities are important?

The drag force: \(F_d\), \([F_d]=M L T^{-2}\)
The velocity with respect to the fluid far away: \(v\), \([v]=L T^{-1}\)
The size of the body: \(r\), \([r]=L\)
The fluid density: \(\rho\), \([\rho]=M L^{-3}\)
The fluid viscosity: \(\eta\), \([\eta]=M L^{-1}T^{-1}\)



Dimensional analysis of drag on a particle
All physical quantities have dimensions. In addition we have measurement units, like the SI units, for all these quantities.






Figure 4: Physical quantities, dimensions and SI units.









NoteBuckingham’s Π theorem



The number of independent dimensionless parameters necessary to describe a system is the number of physical quantities minus the number of independent dimensions.


In our case this gives \(5-3=2\) dimensionless quantities that govern the behaviour of the system.
Let us use the other quantities to make a dimensionless parameter with \(F_d\), starting with \(\rho\): \([F_d/\rho]=T^{-2}L^4\). Then remove the dimension \(T\): \([F_d/\rho v^2]=L^2\), and then \(L\):
\[
C_{R}=\frac{F_d}{\rho v^2r^2}.
\tag{9}\]
\(C_{R}\) is a dimensionless number that we will call the R drag coefficient.
But we may also use \(\eta\) to remove the mass dimension from \(F_d\): \([F_d/\eta]=L^2T^{-1}\). Then we use \(v\) to remove the time, \([F_d/\eta v]=L\), and then the length:
\[
C_{S}=\frac{F_d}{\eta v r}.
\tag{10}\]
\(C_{S}\) is a dimensionless number that we will call the S drag coefficient. The two drag coefficients are pure numbers that depend on the shape of the body. According to Buckingham’s Π theorem we have now found the two dimensionless numbers that are needed to describe the system.


Stokes and Reynolds drag
But these two dimensionless numbers correspond to two very different drag forces. How can they both describe the same physical phenomenon? They describe two different ways the fluid can react to the moving body: either flowing smoothly as a laminar flow around the body, or whirling turbulently in the wake of the body. Let us look at the ratio between the two drag forces:
\[
\frac{F_{dR}}{F_{dS}}=\frac{C_R\rho v^2r^2}{C_S\eta v r}=\frac{C_R\rho vr}{C_S\eta}\approx \frac{\rho vr}{\eta}=Re
\tag{11}\]
The ratio \(F_{dR}/F_{dS}\) is the ratio between the inertial and viscous drag forces. It is called the Reynolds number \(Re\). When \(Re\gg 1\) the inertial (Rayleigh) drag force \(F_{dR}\) dominates. This is the case when the fluid accelerates a lot and becomes turbulent. When \(Re\ll 1\) the viscous (Stokes) drag force \(F_{dS}\) dominates. This is true when the flow is laminar. Stokes drag for a sphere is \(F_{dS}=C_S\eta vr=6\pi\eta vr\).
What is the Reynolds number of the Brownian particles in our experiment? \(Re=\rho vr/\eta\approx 10^3\cdot 10^{-6}\cdot 10^{-6}/10^{-3}=10^{-6}\). They are clearly in the Stokes, low Reynolds number regime.
Sometimes we also use the viscous friction coefficient \(\xi\), defined as the ratio between the drag force and the velocity:
\[
\xi=\frac{F_d}{v}
\tag{12}\]
The viscous friction coefficient in the Stokes regime (\(Re\ll 1\)) for a sphere is \(\xi=6\pi\eta r\).

title: Physics of active and passive motion in biology
text:
Theory of Brownian motion

The childhood of statistical physics
In the early 1900s it became increasingly clear to physicists that the “molecular-kinetic theory”, which described a statistical microscopic basis for thermodynamics, had to prevail. One of the final nails in the coffin for those who opposed it was one of Einstein’s 1905 articles, Investigations on the theory of the Brownian movement. Einstein had been made aware of microscopic observations by the biologist Brown, where small pollen particles in a liquid moved around randomly. Einstein used this as a basis and created a quantitative model where measurable quantities could be compared. It did not take many years before experimentalists were able to measure the different quantities independently. They thus confirmed Einstein’s model, and with it the microscopic theory of heat that we take for granted today.


The Langevin equation: fluctuating forces and fluid friction
In 1908 Langevin published a simpler and more elegant derivation of the model of Brownian motion, Sur la théorie du mouvement brownien. Molecular motion and the equipartition principle are fundamental to the microscopic theory of heat:






NoteThe equipartition principle



The mean kinetic energy of every quadratic degree of freedom of motion is \(kT/2\).


Here \(k\) is the Boltzmann constant and \(T\) the temperature. For the translational velocity \(v_x=dx/dt\) of a molecule in the \(x\)-direction the kinetic energy is
\[
\frac{1}{2}m\langle v_x^2\rangle=\frac{1}{2}kT,
\tag{13}\]
where \(\langle\ldots\rangle\) means the “ensemble average”, the average over many molecules.

Viscous damping
For particles that are much larger than the average distance between the liquid molecules, the liquid can be treated as a continuum and the hydrodynamic damping of the particle motion can be studied. The fluid resistance for a sphere in a viscous liquid at low Reynolds numbers is, as shown above,
\[
F_d=6\pi\eta v_xr,
\]
where \(\eta\) is the shear viscosity of the fluid and \(r\) is the radius of the sphere.


The Langevin equation
The macroscopic particles are subject to a rapidly varying random force \(F_r\) due to the thermal motion of the liquid molecules, and a slowly varying damping force \(F_d\) due to the viscosity of the liquid. Langevin combined these forces into an equation of motion for the particles:
\[
m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=F_r-F_d=F_r-6\pi\eta r\frac{dx}{dt}.
\tag{14}\]
An equation of motion for a system where the force can be divided into a fast-varying and a slowly varying part is called a Langevin equation. By multiplying both sides with \(x\) and using the chain rule, Eq. 14 can be written as
\[
\frac{1}{2}m\left(\frac{d^2x^2}{dt^2}-2v_x^2\right)=xF_r-3\pi\eta r\frac{dx^2}{dt}.
\tag{15}\]


Take the ensemble average and solve the equation
If one takes the ensemble average of Eq. 15, the direct contribution from \(F_r\) disappears, \(\langle xF_r\rangle=0\), because the random force is not correlated with the position of the particle. Using Eq. 13, Eq. 15 can now be written as
\[
\frac{1}{2}m\frac{d^2\langle x^2\rangle}{dt^2}-kT=-3\pi\eta r\frac{d\langle x^2\rangle}{dt}.
\tag{16}\]
This equation can be solved:
\[
\frac{d\langle x^2\rangle}{dt}=\frac{kT}{3\pi\eta r}+Ce^{-6\pi\eta r t/m},
\tag{17}\]
where the last term disappears when \(t\gg m/6\pi\eta r\sim10^{-8}\) s. This means that if we track the positions of many particles and calculate the mean square displacement per unit time, and we know the viscosity and radius of the particles, we can determine Boltzmann’s constant \(k\). Such a determination of \(k\), and its comparison with other methods of determining \(k\), was the first test of Einstein’s model for Brownian motion.


The Einstein relation
Since \(2D=d\langle x^2\rangle/dt\) and \(\xi=6\pi\eta r\), Eq. 17 gives \(d\langle x^2\rangle/dt=kT/(\xi/2)\), and we get the






ImportantEinstein relation



\[
\xi D=kT
\tag{18}\]

title: Physics of active and passive motion in biology
text:
Biological relevance of diffusion

Permeation through a membrane






Figure 5: Permeation through a membrane.



The flux (flow rate per unit area) is \(J_i=\frac{1}{A}\frac{\Delta N_i}{\Delta t}\).
How does \(c_i\) change with time, when \(c_0\) is constant?
\[
\frac{\partial c_i}{\partial t}=-\frac{\partial\Delta c}{\partial t}=\frac{1}{V}\frac{\partial N_i}{\partial t}=\frac{3}{r}J_i
\]
because \(A=4\pi r^2\), \(V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), \(V/A=r/3\). The permeability \(P\) is defined by \(J=P\Delta c\). We can enter this into the above equation and solve:
\[
\begin{aligned}
-\frac{d\Delta c}{dt}&=\frac{3}{r}P\Delta c\\
\int_{\Delta c_0}^{\Delta c}\frac{d\Delta c}{\Delta c}&=-\frac{3P}{r}\int_0^t dt\\
\ln\Delta c-\ln\Delta c_0&=-\frac{3P}{r}t\\
\frac{\Delta c}{\Delta c_0}&=e^{-t/\tau}, \qquad \tau=\frac{r}{3P}.
\end{aligned}
\]






Figure 6: Diffusion through a membrane with low partition coefficient.



Permeation is diffusion through the membrane plus resistance to entry and exit. The partition coefficient \(B\) is
\[
B=\frac{\text{solubility in oil}}{\text{solubility in water}}
\]
Diffusion in the membrane gives
\[
J=-D\frac{dc}{dx}=\frac{DB\Delta c}{L}=P\Delta c
\quad \Rightarrow \quad P=\frac{DB}{L}
\]
Then the time constant can be written
\[
\tau=\frac{rL}{3DB}
\]
Some numbers:

Partition coefficient of water in a lipid bilayer membrane: \(B=4.2\cdot 10^{-5}\) (A. Finkelstein, J. Gen. Physiol. 68, 127 (1976)).
Thickness of the cell membrane: \(L=7.5\)–\(10\) nm (BioNumbers).
This gives a permeability of \(P=10^{-9}\cdot 4\cdot 10^{-5}/10^{-8}\) m/s \(\approx 4\) µm/s.
And a time constant for permeation of water into a cell with radius 10 µm of \(\tau=r/(3P)\approx 1\) s. That’s pretty fast!
The partition coefficient of monovalent ions is \(B\approx 10^{-60}\). That’s why cells need ion channels.



Oxygen diffusion limit on microbial metabolism
See Nelson 4.6.2, p. 138.

Oxygen is consumed by the microbe.
Oxygen is transported from outside:

lakes, ocean: turbulent flow
ECM, ponds: diffusion

Assume instant uptake at the microbial surface.







Figure 7: In steady state the same current flows through spheres of all radii.



\[
\begin{aligned}
J(r)=\frac{I}{4\pi r^2}&=-D\frac{dc}{dr}\\
-\frac{I\, dr}{4\pi r^2}&=D\, dc\\
\frac{I}{4\pi }\left.\frac{1}{r}\right|_{r_0}^\infty&=D \left. c\right|_{0}^{c_\infty}\\
\frac{I}{4\pi}\frac{1}{r_0}&=Dc_\infty\\
I&=4\pi Dc_\infty r_0
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the maximum rate at which O\(_2\) can be consumed by any bacterium whatsoever.






Figure 8: Concentration distribution around a consuming bacterium.



So the maximum O\(_2\) diffusion rate scales linearly with the radius \(r\) of the microbe. How does the consumption rate scale with the size of the organism? A first guess would be \(I\propto r^3\). But there is an empirical relationship called Kleiber’s law, shown to be valid all the way down to microbe size: \(I\propto M^{0.75}\), where \(M\) is the mass of the organism. Since \(M\propto r^3\), the scaling is \(I\propto r^{9/4}=r^{2.25}\) (T. E. Riedel, W. M. Berelson, K. H. Nealson, S. E. Finkel, Appl. Environ. Microbiol. 79, 4921 (2013)).






Figure 9: Scaling of consumption and transport rate with bacterium size.



Plotting the scaling of consumption and transport rate against microbe size, one finds that there must be an upper limit to the size \(r_{\rm max}\) of a microbe that does not swim or live in a turbulent world.


Size of eukaryotes and prokaryotes
Here is another nice and simple paper to analyse.

title: B: Entropy, ions and membranes
text: Why does a cell burst in pure water? How can entropy create forces and order? Why is there a voltage across every cell membrane, and why does it cost the cell so much energy to keep it? We build up from multiplicity and the Boltzmann distribution to free energy, entropic forces, osmosis, the Nernst potential, Donnan equilibrium and ion pumps.

title: Elective projects
text: After the common project P1, you choose one elective in each round. Every elective follows the same four milestones as P1 (running, validated core figure, report with LLM log, oral defense). Each one has its own validation step: a way of showing that your result is right.

title: Elective projects
text:
Round 1 (P2): weeks 11–17
Choose by Sunday 14 March. Report due Sunday 25 April, defense Tuesday 27 April.
2A Freezing cells: the physics of cryopreservation. Osmosis, freezing-point depression and water flow through the membrane during cooling. Find the cooling rate that avoids both ice inside the cell and damage from concentrated solution. Possibly with a wet-lab measurement of cell volume against osmolarity.
2B Nerve signals: from Nernst to Hodgkin–Huxley. From the resting potential to the action potential and neuronal calcium dynamics, compared with two-photon calcium imaging in mouse cortex.
2C Active cell layers: from Vicsek to epithelia. Map the flocking transition in the Vicsek model, then measure cell shape, orientation and nematic order in quantitative-phase images of epithelial monolayers, tested against null models.

title: Elective projects
text:
Round 2 (P3): weeks 17–21
Choose by Thursday 22 April. Report due Sunday 23 May, defense Tuesday 25 May.
3A Cell sorting and tissue shape with the Cellular Potts model. Reproduce sorting, engulfment and mosaic patterns from contact energies and map the phase diagram.
3B Mechanics of epithelial monolayers (wet lab). Grow epithelial monolayers, image them live, and measure velocity fields and correlation lengths.
3C Imaging at the physical limits. Label-free quantitative phase imaging: from phase to dry mass, calibrated on beads and applied to cells. How do shot noise and photodamage limit what we can see, and what could squeezed light gain?
Detailed project texts will be posted before each elective fair.

title: Working with LLMs
text: In this course you are expected to use large language models (LLMs) such as GPT UiO: for setting up Python, writing and debugging analysis code, understanding methods, and writing reports. This is how much research and technical work is done today. What the course assesses is your own understanding, and that is checked in the oral defenses and the final exam.

title: Working with LLMs
section: What an LLM is good and bad at here
text:
What an LLM is good and bad at here
Good at: installing packages and fixing error messages, writing first versions of analysis code, explaining what a function or a parameter does, suggesting how to plot or fit something, and turning your notes into readable text.
Bad at: knowing what your data look like, knowing whether a number is physically reasonable, and noticing when code runs but gives the wrong answer. It will often answer confidently when it is wrong.

title: Working with LLMs
text:
Five habits

Give it the physics and the numbers. “Beads of 0.51 µm, 0.1837 µm per pixel, 15 fps, I expect D ≈ 0.9 µm²/s” gets you far better help than “how do I use trackpy?”.
Ask it to explain, not only to write. For every step, ask why. If you cannot explain a line of your code, you do not yet own it.
Test on data with a known answer. Synthetic data, a limiting case, a simple estimate. If the method fails there, it fails on your data too.
Estimate before you compute. Know the order of magnitude you expect before you look at the result.
Keep a log. Note what you asked, what went wrong and how you found out. It becomes the LLM log in your report and good material for the defense.

title: Working with LLMs
section: The LLM log in your reports
text:
The LLM log in your reports
One page appended to each report:

What you used an LLM for (code, debugging, explanations, writing).
At least one example where it was wrong, misleading or incomplete, and how you found out.
What you checked yourself, and how.

The log is not graded on how much or how little you used an LLM. It shows that you know where the result comes from.

title: Working with LLMs
text:
Data and privacy
Use GPT UiO or another tool approved by UiO for anything that includes data or text that is not yours to share. Do not paste personal information into any LLM.
